notes.meaning: Jacob heard the report that grain was available in Egypt, likely seeing what his neighbors had brought home. He urged his sons to stop sitting around looking at one another in helpless hesitation.
Jacob told his sons to travel down to Egypt to buy food so their family would not starve. Even though God could provide miraculously, Jacob used ordinary, sensible means to preserve their lives.
Ten of Joseph's brothers set out together for Egypt to buy grain. They went in person rather than sending servants, perhaps for safety or because more men could purchase more food.
Jacob refused to let Benjamin travel with his older brothers. Benjamin had taken Joseph's special place in his father's heart, and Jacob feared that a deadly accident might take him too.
The sons of Jacob arrived in Egypt among crowds of other travelers in need. The severe drought covered Canaan as well, forcing many families to make the long desert journey to buy food.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern critical scholars view the repeated mention of the famine as evidence that different written sources were joined together.

notes.meaning: Joseph held supreme power in Egypt and personally oversaw the grain sales to foreigners. When his brothers entered, they bowed low with their faces to the ground, fulfilling the prophetic dreams Joseph had years before.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early Catholic teaching noted that Joseph wisely sold the grain rather than handing it out freely, ensuring that the supply would last for everyone.

notes.meaning: Joseph recognized his brothers immediately, but he acted like a stranger and spoke sternly to them. He was not seeking personal revenge, but wanted to test their character and discover what had happened to his family.
Joseph knew them at once, but the brothers had no idea who he was. More than twenty years had passed, and Joseph was dressed in Egyptian robes, spoke their language, and ruled with great authority.
Seeing them bow reminded Joseph of the dreams God had given him in his youth. He accused them of being spies sent to inspect the undefended borders and weak spots of Egypt.
The brothers quickly denied the charge and addressed Joseph with great respect. They explained that their only purpose was to purchase food so their families could survive.
The men pointed out that they were all sons of one father. No single family would ever risk ten sons at once on a dangerous spy mission.
Joseph repeated the accusation, insisting that they had come to see where the country was unprotected. He maintained this harsh stance to press them for more details about their home.

To defend their honesty, the brothers shared more about their household in Canaan. They explained that they had originally been twelve brothers, but the youngest was at home with their father, and one was gone.
Joseph declared that their story only confirmed his suspicion that they were spies. He continued playing the stern ruler to keep them off balance and lead them toward genuine reflection.
Joseph set a strict test to prove whether they were telling the truth. Swearing by the life of Pharaoh, he declared that they would not leave Egypt until their youngest brother came there.

Joseph initially demanded that they choose one brother to go back and fetch Benjamin while the rest remained locked in prison. This would reveal whether their claim about their family was real or a lie.
Joseph locked all ten brothers in prison for three days. This brief confinement gave them time to think and let them feel a small taste of the helplessness they had once forced upon him.
On the third day, Joseph offered them an easier way to live. He told them he feared God, reassuring them that a ruler who answers to the true God will deal fairly.
Joseph reversed his earlier plan so that only one brother had to stay behind in custody. He told the other nine to take grain home to keep their hungry families from starving.
Joseph commanded them to bring back their youngest brother to verify their words and save their lives. Having no other choice, the brothers accepted his terms.
Under this sudden pressure, the brothers began to connect their troubles to their past cruelty. They remembered seeing Joseph's deep agony and how they had ignored his desperate pleas for mercy.
Reuben reminded the others that he had urged them not to harm the boy. Because they had refused to listen to his warning, he said God was now requiring an accounting for Joseph's blood.
The brothers did not realize that Joseph understood every word they said. He had been using an Egyptian interpreter to conceal his true language and background from them.
Hearing their remorse moved Joseph so deeply that he had to step away and weep in secret. When he composed himself and returned, he picked Simeon and had him bound before their eyes as a hostage.

Joseph gave secret orders to fill their bags with grain, return each man's silver inside his sack, and supply them with food for the road. He showed generous care for his family while keeping his identity hidden.
The brothers loaded their donkeys with the grain and started their journey home. They were relieved to be free, but weighed down by the loss of Simeon and the hard road ahead.
At their stopping place for the night, one brother opened his sack to feed his donkey. He was shocked to find his money sitting right at the top of the sack.
The discovery made their hearts sink in terror. Because their consciences were already awake to their past sins, they feared this strange turn of events was God's punishment catching up with them.
The brothers arrived home to their father Jacob in Canaan. They immediately gave him a full report of everything that had happened during their trip to Egypt.
They recounted how the lord of the land had spoken roughly to them. They explained that he had accused them of spying on the country's weaknesses.
They told Jacob how they had defended themselves before the governor. They insisted that they were honest, peaceful men on a simple errand to buy food.
They described how they had shared their family history to clear their names. They had told the ruler that they were twelve brothers, with the youngest still in Canaan and one gone.
They explained the harsh condition the ruler had set to prove their innocence. He had kept one brother as a prisoner and sent the rest home with grain for their hungry families.
The ruler promised that if they brought Benjamin back, he would release Simeon and allow them to trade freely in Egypt. This left the family with an agonizing decision to make.
As they emptied out their sacks, each man found his full bundle of silver right inside. Seeing the returned money filled both the brothers and their father with dread.

Jacob broke down in bitter sorrow, blaming his sons for bringing disaster upon him. He mourned that Joseph was gone, Simeon was captive, and now Benjamin was at risk, feeling as though everything was against him.

Reuben tried to ease his father's anxiety by offering his own two sons as a guarantee, saying Jacob could kill them if he failed to return Benjamin. Reuben meant to show deep commitment, but it was a rash and foolish proposal.

Jacob firmly refused to let Benjamin travel with them, clinging to the last child left from his beloved Rachel. He warned that if any harm came to Benjamin, the crushing heartbreak would drive him straight to the grave.
